draft.title: Learning from Europe
card: Some cities overseas have found ways to improve liveability. Planners in other places can study them and borrow ideas.
Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, built safe bike lanes that are kept apart from traffic. It also made some streets car-free, so people can walk and spend time there.
An idea that works in one city may not work in another. Climate, distance, population and money can all differ.
Australian cities can judge whether an idea would suit them before they copy it. Many have trialled bike lanes and car-free streets.
draft.remember: Good ideas from Copenhagen can be tested for fit before an Australian city uses them.

a.q: What did Copenhagen do that other cities have studied?
opts: Built safe bike lanes and car-free streets
Banned all buses from the city centre
Moved homes far away from shops
Closed its parks to build roads
a.why: Copenhagen is known for safe bike lanes kept apart from traffic and for car-free streets. The other options are not ideas it used to improve liveability.
a.clue: Think about how Copenhagen helps people walk and cycle.

b.q: A council in the Northern Territory wants to copy Copenhagen's bike lanes. What should it do first?
opts: Judge whether the idea suits its local climate and needs
Build the same lanes at once, since they worked in Denmark
Drop the idea, since no overseas idea can work in Australia
Wait until every other city has copied the idea first
b.why: Places differ in climate, distance and money, so the council should judge fit before it builds. Copying at once ignores those differences. Dropping the idea is also wrong, because Australian cities have used overseas ideas.
b.clue: Ideas need to fit the local place.

a.best: Built safe bike lanes and car-free streets

b.best: Judge whether the idea suits its local climate and needs

proposal.title: Learning from Europe
card: Some cities overseas have found ways to improve liveability. Planners in other places can study them and borrow ideas.

Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark, built bike lanes that are kept apart from car traffic. Riders feel safer, so more people choose to cycle. It also made some streets car-free, so people can walk and spend time there.
An idea that works in one city may not work in another. Climate, distance, population and money can all differ.
Australian cities can judge whether an idea would suit them before they copy it. Some have trialled bike lanes and car-free streets.
proposal.remember: Good ideas from Copenhagen can be tested for fit before an Australian city uses them.

a.q: Copenhagen keeps its bike lanes apart from car traffic. How does this make the city more liveable?
opts: Cycling feels safer, so more people choose to ride
Cars can drive faster with bikes out of the way
The city needs fewer footpaths for people walking
Buses no longer need set routes through the city
a.why: Lanes kept apart from cars make riders feel safe, so more people cycle. The aim is to help people, not to speed up cars, so faster driving is not the reason.
a.clue: Think about the people on the bikes, not the cars.

b.clue: Ideas need to fit the local place.
